a1.title: Poems on Bus Tickets
a1.excerpt: In one city, every bus ticket has a short poem on it.
a1.body:
Ana is a bus driver. She drives the number 7 bus. In the morning, people are tired and quiet.

Ana has an idea. Every bus ticket has a short poem now. People in the city write the poems.

The city has more than 2,000 poems! One poet is 7 years old. One poet is 94.

Every Friday, Ana reads a poem to everyone.

Now people talk on the bus. They talk about the poems. Some people keep their tickets.

a2.title: A City Puts Poems on Its Bus Tickets
a2.excerpt: A bus driver wanted happier mornings, so now every ticket in the city has a short poem.
a2.body:
Ana is 52 and drives the number 7 bus. She started this job twenty years ago. Every morning, she saw tired, quiet passengers with their phones.

Last winter, she had an idea. She asked the bus company for something new. She wanted a short poem on every ticket. The company said yes.

Anyone in the city can write a poem. But it must have only four lines. In March, the first poems appeared on the tickets. In six months, people sent more than 2,000 poems! The youngest poet is 7 years old, and the oldest is 94.

Every Friday morning, Ana reads the week's poem to her passengers. They clap when she finishes.

Now people on the bus talk to each other about the poems. Some passengers collect the tickets. “People smile more now,” Ana said.

b1.title: A Bus Driver's Idea Puts a Poem on Every Ticket
b1.excerpt: Since March, every bus ticket in one small city has come with a four-line poem by a local resident — and the morning ride has never been the same.
b1.body:
For twenty years, Ana Ruiz has driven the number 7 bus through a small city, and for most of that time the morning journey was the same: tired passengers, grey faces and total silence, apart from the sound of phones.

“I kept thinking there must be a way to wake people up gently,” she says. Last winter, she suggested an unusual idea to the bus company: why not print a short poem on the back of every ticket?

To her surprise, the company agreed. Anyone living in the city was invited to send in a poem of no more than four lines. A small group of volunteers, including a retired teacher and two secondary school students, chooses a new poem each week.

The first poems appeared in March. Since then, the city has received more than 2,000 poems. The youngest poet is seven years old; the oldest is 94. Topics range from rainy Mondays to lost umbrellas and first love.

Every Friday morning, Ana reads the poem of the week over the bus speakers. Passengers have started clapping when she finishes.

The tickets have become so popular that some people collect them, and the library now holds a ticket swap every Sunday. Next year, the city plans to publish the best hundred poems in a free book.

“People used to look at their phones,” Ana says. “Now they look at their tickets — and then at each other.”

b2.title: Four Lines for the Morning Commute: The Bus Tickets That Turned a City Into Poets
b2.excerpt: A veteran bus driver's hunch that her silent morning passengers needed something to talk about has produced more than 2,000 poems, a weekly Friday reading and an unexpected city-wide craze.
b2.body:
Ana Ruiz has been driving the number 7 bus for twenty years, and she knows the morning commute better than anyone. For most of that time, she said, it had been a picture of quiet exhaustion: rows of sleepy faces, lit only by the glow of phone screens.

“I kept wondering whether something small could change the mood,” she explained. Last winter, she approached the city's bus company with a suggestion that, by her own admission, she expected to be laughed at: why not print a short poem on the back of every ticket?

Rather than laughing, the company's managers agreed to a trial. Residents were invited to submit poems of no more than four lines, and a panel of volunteers — among them a retired literature teacher and two sixth-form students — was set up to select a new poem each week.

The response has been extraordinary. Since the first tickets were printed in March, more than 2,000 poems have been received, from writers ranging in age from seven to ninety-four. Subjects vary widely, from rainy Mondays and forgotten umbrellas to first love and the particular joy of catching a bus just as the doors close.

Every Friday, Ana reads the poem of the week over the bus's speakers. What began as a slightly nervous announcement has become something of a ritual: passengers now applaud, and regulars have been known to request encores.

The tickets themselves have taken on a life of their own. Some commuters collect every edition, and the central library has started hosting a Sunday ticket swap, where collectors trade missing poems. The city has also announced that the best hundred poems will be published next year in a free pocket-sized anthology.

Not everyone was won over immediately. One passenger admitted that, if she had been asked beforehand, she would have called the scheme “a waste of good ink”. “Now I check the back of my ticket before I even sit down,” she said.

For Ana, the change is visible every morning. “People used to stare at their phones,” she said. “Now they read their tickets — and then they look up and talk to each other.”

c1.title: Verse on the Number 7: How a Bus Driver's Modest Proposal Turned a City's Commuters Into Poets
c1.excerpt: When a veteran driver suggested printing four-line poems on the backs of bus tickets, few expected the idea to last a month; six months and more than 2,000 submissions later, the morning commute has acquired an unlikely literary life.
c1.body:
Anyone who has driven the same bus route for twenty years develops an acute sense of its moods. For Ana Ruiz, who has steered the number 7 through the city's narrow streets for two decades, the dominant mood of the morning run had long been one of collective resignation: rows of drowsy faces, illuminated by phone screens, and a silence broken only by the hiss of the doors.

“I used to wonder whether there was anything small enough to be practical, but big enough to make people look up,” she recalls. Last winter, she put a proposal to the city's bus company that she fully expected to be politely declined: why not print a short poem on the back of every ticket?

To her astonishment, management agreed to a trial. Residents were invited to submit verses of no more than four lines, and a volunteer panel — comprising, among others, a retired literature teacher, a librarian and two sixth-form students — was convened to select a new poem each week. The brief was deliberately loose. “We ask for four lines and a bit of warmth,” one panel member explains. “Beyond that, the city decides what it wants to say.”

What it wants to say, it transpires, is a great deal. Since the first tickets rolled off the press in March, more than 2,000 poems have arrived, from authors ranging in age from seven to ninety-four. Their subjects are gloriously eclectic: the quiet tragedy of lost umbrellas, the small triumph of catching a bus as its doors begin to close, a grandmother's recipe rendered in rhyming couplets, and, on at least one occasion, an extended metaphor comparing the ring road to a sleeping dragon.

Choosing a single poem each week has proved the panel's most agonising task. Submissions are read anonymously, spread across the librarian's kitchen table and debated with a seriousness that one member likens to a jury deliberation conducted over biscuits. The youngest published poet, a seven-year-old who contributed four lines about a bus that dreams of becoming a boat, has since been invited to read her work aloud on the route. The oldest, a ninety-four-year-old former tram conductor, submitted a gently wry verse about the city as it looked from the back platform seventy years ago — and now receives fan mail at the depot.

Every Friday, Ana reads the week's poem over the bus's speakers. The first readings, she admits, were delivered with considerable trepidation. Now they are something closer to a ritual: passengers applaud, regulars occasionally request encores, and at least one commuter has been spotted recording the performance for a relative who has since moved away.

The tickets, meanwhile, have become collectable in their own right. Enthusiasts hoard complete runs; the central library now hosts a Sunday swap at which collectors barter for elusive editions; and the city has confirmed that the hundred most popular poems will be published next year as a free pocket anthology, to be distributed, fittingly, on board.

Not everyone was an instant convert. “Had you asked me in February, I'd have told you it was a waste of perfectly good ink,” one passenger confesses. “These days I read the back of my ticket before I've even found a seat.” Such reversals are, for the scheme's organisers, the most gratifying measure of success.

For Ana, the evidence is visible in her mirror every morning. “People used to disappear into their phones,” she says. “Now they read their tickets, and then — this is the bit I love — they look up and say something to whoever is sitting next to them.”
